examples.label: unix-privesc-check — manual alternative to linpeas (no external binary needed)
examples.command:
./unix-privesc-check standard > output.txt
grep WARNING output.txt
# WARNING: /etc/passwd is a critical config file. World write is set for /etc/passwd

notes: Tools: LinPEAS, LinEnum, linuxprivchecker, Seatbelt, JAWS. Refs: GTFOBins, LOLBAS, HackTricks, PayloadsAllTheThings.
name: Privilege Escalation - Enumeration Basics
description: First moves after a foothold: run an enumeration script and check the obvious wins - installed packages, sudo rights, and readable configs with credentials.

defense.why_it_works: Post-exploitation enumeration inventories the host's configuration and the current user's privileges — OS/kernel version, users, groups, sudo rights, SUID binaries, cron jobs — to find a path from a low-privileged foothold to root/SYSTEM.
defense.prerequisites: An initial foothold (any shell) on the target host.
defense.impact: A map of privilege-escalation opportunities: writable sensitive files, misconfigured sudo, SUID/SGID binaries, scheduled tasks, and stored credentials.
defense.detection: Automated enumeration scripts like LinPEAS run many commands associated with vulnerability identification and create significant 'noise' that may trigger antivirus or security monitoring software watching for these event patterns. In some cases this will prevent the script from running or trigger an alert that the system has been compromised.
defense.artifacts: A burst of enumeration commands (whoami, id, uname, sudo -l, find / -perm) in shell history and process-creation logs; automated enum scripts (e.g. linpeas) touching many files rapidly.
defense.evasion: Run individual manual enumeration commands instead of automated scripts to avoid generating the volume of suspicious events that triggers security tooling.
defense.misconfiguration: Common introductory misconfigurations: services running as root/SYSTEM unnecessarily, default credentials unchanged, unnecessary services listening on all interfaces, lack of firewall rules exposing services externally, no monitoring or alerting on authentication failures.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Service listening on all interfaces with default creds (common in labs/staging):
ss -tlnp | grep LISTEN
# 0.0.0.0:21  (FTP on all interfaces)
# 0.0.0.0:3306 (MySQL on all interfaces — should be 127.0.0.1 only)
# 0.0.0.0:8080 (Tomcat with manager app accessible)

# Running services as root:
ps aux | grep -E '(mysql|apache|nginx|ftp)'
# root  1234  /usr/sbin/mysqld  <-- should run as 'mysql' user
defense.secure_config:
# Bind services to localhost or specific IPs (not 0.0.0.0):
# MySQL: my.cnf -> bind-address = 127.0.0.1
# Apache: Listen 127.0.0.1:80 (if behind a proxy)

# Run services as dedicated low-priv users:
# systemd unit: User=mysql Group=mysql

# Host-based firewall (ufw):
ufw default deny incoming
ufw allow from 10.10.1.0/24 to any port 22  # SSH from mgmt only
ufw allow 443  # HTTPS
ufw enable

# Change all default credentials immediately after installation
# Enable fail2ban for SSH and web services
